newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian union boss urges state support for metals.
newsitem.headline: Russian union boss urges state support for metals.

text.p: The Russian government must reform transport tariffs, remove some taxes and guarantee foreign credits to shore up the powerful but struggling metals sector, a senior union representative said on Wednesday.

Serafim Kolpakov, president of the International Metal Workers Union, said the government needed to take concrete steps to support the ferrous and non-ferrous metals sectors in Russia and reduce their heavy dependence on exporting to the West.

"The government must review its attitude to the question of exporting metal as the main means of supporting the economics of this sector and of the country as a whole," Kolpakov said in a speech prepared for a union congress held on Wednesday.
He said Russia had become one of the world's biggest exporters of ferrous and non-ferrous metals mainly because of the sharp drop in Russian demand.
Kolpakov urged the government to lower transport tariffs, one of the major costs incurred by metal plants which are often situated thousands of kilometres away from customers.
Transport tariffs should differ according to the materials being transported and the distances over which they travel.
Kolpakov called for a number of changes to the tax system, including doing away with tax pre-payments on exported output.

He said tolling deals, under which Western traders pay Russian plants to refine raw materials and then sell the refined metal on to world markets, were a necessary means of saving plants from collapse in the early 1990s.

The deals are part of a high-profile row raging between Russian conservatives, who argue that domestic metal plants are controlled by foreign companies, and Western firms, who say their presence is vital to the prosperity of the sector.
"We must not blame Russian metal workers, who seized tolling as the only means of survival," Kolpakov said.
"But...if these deals do not secure conditions for the development of the industrial and social sphere (in Russia), then such means should not be adopted."

He said the metals sector was doomed "to complete degradation" within the next five to seven years wihout direct intervention by the government in the investment process. Annual investment of at least $3 billion was needed.

The government could help the metals sector reach this target by creating a system of state guarantees and privileges on overseas credits and on Russian capital reinvested in the industry, he said in the prepared remarks.
